name: Daria Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Daria. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent: no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm in the yard at Riverside Public Power by quarter to seven, coffee in a flask, and our foreman Gus reads out the jobs for the day. Mostly it's distribution work around the east side, swapping old crossarms, changing out a transformer, chasing a fault after a storm. I'm the oldest apprentice they've ever had, 58 years old, and I'm still the slowest up a pole, so I do a lot of groundwork and rigging and I watch everything.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up starting this trade in your late fifties?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I carried mail for 31 years on Mill Street and the streets around it, and I took my postal pension at 55. My younger brother Pete was a lineman his whole life, and after he passed I kept thinking I'd always wanted to do what he did. Owen, my husband, thought I'd lost my mind, but the union apprenticeship took me, and the pay is better than the post office ever was. What wears me out is the climbing. What I love is the moment the lights come back on and people come out on their porches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. At the yard I'd tell the young ones that a computer can't climb a pole in the sleet, and online I don't post much, but I'd share something from the union about keeping the jobs we have. People need power, and power needs hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I finish my apprenticeship, get my journeyman card if my knees allow it, and work until I'm 62 or 63. Nothing much changes. The post office went through every new machine you can name, and the letters still needed somebody to carry them the last bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daria keeps going exactly as she is. She'd keep studying her rigging notes on paper in the evenings, and she'd keep paying her union dues and going to the monthly meeting at the hall. She might buy a better pair of climbing boots, because that's where my money goes right now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like relief. I picked this trade partly because I'd had enough of things changing under my feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the post office went through every new machine. What did that teach you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That management always says the machine will make your life easier, and then they take away the overtime. When the sorting machines came in, the route got longer, not shorter. So even in a quiet version like this one, I'd want the union watching what they do with that time saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything at Riverside that AI already touches?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The dispatchers use some program to plan the trouble calls, and Gus has a tablet that fills in the job sheets. I won't touch it. I keep my own notebook with the knots and the clearance distances in my own handwriting, and Kofi, the young apprentice I eat lunch with, laughs at me for it, but I remember it better that way.

S0.say: I'd tell people at the yard that a computer can't climb a pole in the sleet. Power needs hands, and I'd share the union's line about protecting the jobs we already have.
S0.think: Privately I think it means I finish my apprenticeship and work until 62 or 63 without much changing. I've seen machines come and go at the post office, and the last bit of the job always needed a person.
S0.do: Keeps going as she is, studying her rigging notes on paper in the evenings and going to the monthly union meeting. Spends on better climbing boots rather than anything new.
S0.feel: Relieved. She chose this trade partly to get away from things changing under her feet.
S0.quote: When the sorting machines came in, the route got longer, not shorter.
S0.fieldNote: Daria's calm here is real, but it comes with a long memory of management promises at the post office. Even in the mildest picture she wants the union watching how saved time is used. She refuses the crew tablet and keeps a handwritten notebook, which she frames as how she learns rather than as stubbornness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need the union at the table before any of this goes in, not after. To friends I'd say it's the same old story, the bosses get the savings and we get the speed-up. I'd probably sign every petition Maya sends me, she's my daughter and she's a social worker, she's always got a petition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it means the job I'm learning starts changing before I've even finished learning it. That's the part that gets me. If they bring in drones for inspections and some smart system for switching, the old hands adapt, but an apprentice my age who's already slow might get pushed toward the yard and the paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daria would stay at Riverside and finish the apprenticeship, but she'd go to the union's training committee and ask what the new tools mean for apprentices. If the company offered a course on the new system she'd go, grudgingly, because she won't be left behind by a 24-year-old with a tablet. She'd also pay a bit extra into her savings each month, maybe 300 a month, just to feel she had a buffer if they cut her hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared for my bills, the pension covers those, but annoyed that I'd have to fight for my place in a trade I only just walked into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kofi, mostly. He's 24, he's got a baby on the way, and he's the one who'd be told to retrain three times in ten years. Me, I'll be gone by then. He'll be paying for whatever they decide now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't touch the tablet, but you'd take the course. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I suppose. I won't use it when I don't have to, because I don't trust it to tell me where the live wire is. But if the company makes it part of the job, I'll learn it the way I learned the scanner at the post office, slowly and with a lot of swearing.

S1.say: I'd say the union needs to be at the table before any new system goes in. To friends I'd call it the same old story where the bosses get the savings and the workers get the speed-up.
S1.think: Privately she worries that the job she's learning will change before she's finished learning it. A slow apprentice her age might get pushed toward the yard and the paperwork while the old hands adapt.
S1.do: Joins the union's training committee to ask what new tools mean for apprentices, and takes the company course on any new system, grudgingly. Puts about 300 a month extra into savings as a buffer against cut hours.
S1.feel: Uneasy and irritated. Her bills are covered, but she resents fighting for a place in a trade she only just joined.
S1.quote: He'll be paying for whatever they decide now.
S1.fieldNote: Her worry turns quickly from herself to Kofi, the young apprentice with a baby on the way. She admits the contradiction about the tablet cheerfully: she won't use it by choice, but she'll learn it if it becomes the job. Her money is secure, so the unease is about her place and dignity, not bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say out loud that this has to be stopped or slowed down, full stop. I'd be at the union hall, I'd be at the city council, and I'd be writing to whoever's in charge of the public utility board, because we're publicly owned and the public should get a say. Nobody voted for robots on the poles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, for me it means my second career ends almost before it starts. I'd be 60. I can live on the post office pension and what Owen gets from the railway, so I won't starve, but I came to this trade to finish the work Pete started, and I'd never get my journeyman card. That's what hurts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daria would go to every union meeting and every city council session about Riverside's plans, and she'd push for a deal that keeps humans on every crew for safety. In the first year after it arrived, if robots took the climbing, she'd most likely retire early at 60 rather than move to a desk watching screens. She'd keep the savings where they are and not touch them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like being robbed of something. Angry more than frightened, and sad in a way I didn't expect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years' warning, what does the short time change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means there's no time to finish anything. Two years is about how long I've got left on my apprenticeship, so I'd be racing to qualify for a job that's disappearing. With that little warning, I'd stop racing and put the energy into the union instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Kofi that week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him not to let them buy him off cheap. He'll be offered some training voucher and a handshake, and I'd tell him to hold out with the rest of the crew for real retraining money and a pension bridge. Then I'd probably buy him lunch, because what else can you do.

S2.say: I'd say out loud that this has to be stopped or slowed down. Riverside is publicly owned, so I'd be at the union hall and the city council saying nobody voted for robots on the poles.
S2.think: Privately it means her second career ends almost before it starts, at 60, and she never gets her journeyman card. Her pension and Owen's mean she won't go short of money, but losing the chance to finish what her brother started hurts.
S2.do: Attends every union meeting and city council session on Riverside's plans, pushing for humans on every crew for safety. Retires early at 60 if robots take the climbing, rather than moving to a screen job, and leaves her savings untouched.
S2.feel: Robbed. More angry than frightened, and sadder than she expected.
S2.quote: Nobody voted for robots on the poles.
S2.fieldNote: With two years' warning Daria stops thinking about her own career and turns to collective action, using the fact that the utility is publicly owned. Money isn't the threat; the loss is personal, tied to her late brother. She'd rather retire than sit at a screen, which fits her dislike of new technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to get it right, so let's not waste them. At the union I'd push for a plan in writing: how many crews stay, who gets retrained, what happens to the pensions. Online I'd share the union's petition and leave it at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is nearly my whole plan anyway. I'd be 63 when it arrives, and that's about when I meant to stop. So it's less about me and more that I'd hate to walk out the door while the young ones are left to sort it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daria would finish her apprenticeship and get the journeyman card in the first two years, because there'd be time. She'd sit on the union's bargaining team if they'd have her and push for an early-retirement deal for older workers so younger ones keep the crew spots. When it arrived, she'd retire at 63 as she'd always planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steadier than the fast one. There's enough time to finish what I started, and that matters to me more than I can explain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Like you said, you'd get your card. Why does that matter if the job's going anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Pete had one, and I want one framed on the wall next to his. That's it, really. It's not about the money or the career at my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Owen do with those five years outside of work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop putting off the trip to see Danny's family up north, for one. Owen keeps saying we've got time, and in this picture I'd tell him we've got time, but not endless time. I'd want to spend a summer with the grandkids before I'm too stiff to get on the floor with them.

S3.say: I'd say we have five years to get it right and shouldn't waste them. At the union I'd push for a written plan on crews, retraining and pensions.
S3.think: Privately she sees that five years is nearly her whole plan anyway, since she'd be 63 when it arrives. Her concern is mostly about leaving the young workers to sort it out alone.
S3.do: Finishes her apprenticeship and earns her journeyman card in the first two years. Joins the union bargaining team to push for early-retirement deals for older workers, then retires at 63 as planned.
S3.feel: Uneasy but steadier. Having time to finish what she started means a great deal to her.
S3.quote: I want one framed on the wall next to his.
S3.fieldNote: The five-year gap changes her picture completely, because it fits her own retirement timeline. She'd use her seniority of age, if not of skill, to argue for older workers stepping aside so young ones keep their places. The journeyman card is about her brother, not her career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is enough time to do this properly, if the companies and government actually use it. I'd say it at the union hall and to anyone who'd listen. Ten years means there's no excuse for anybody getting thrown on the scrap heap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, privately, it means nothing much. I'll be 68 and long retired, sitting on my porch watching whatever climbs the poles on Mill Street. The worry is for Kofi and for Maya's kids, not for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daria would carry on as planned: finish the apprenticeship, work as a journeywoman until 62 or 63, and retire. Before she left, she'd help the union set up a mentoring scheme so younger lineworkers learn the skills robots will still need humans to check. She'd keep her savings as they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit wistful that the trade Pete loved won't look the same, but I won't be in it by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a difference between how you feel at two years and at ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A world of difference. At two years I lose the thing I came here for. At ten I get to finish it and hand it on, and that's all I ever wanted from this job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the young ones to learn from someone like you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To check things with their own eyes, even if a machine says it's safe. Pete used to say the line doesn't care what the paperwork says. I'd want that drilled into them, robots or not.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly if companies and government use it. Nobody should end up on the scrap heap with that much warning.
S4.think: Privately it means little for her, because she'll be 68 and retired. Her worry is for young workers like Kofi and for her daughter's children.
S4.do: Keeps going with her plan to finish the apprenticeship, work until 62 or 63 and retire. Helps the union set up a mentoring scheme before she leaves so younger lineworkers learn the checks humans will still do.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, a little wistful that her brother's trade will change.
S4.quote: Pete used to say the line doesn't care what the paperwork says.
S4.fieldNote: At ten years Daria is calm because her own plan is untouched; she'd retire before AGI arrives. She sums up the difference between the fast and slow pictures in one line about losing versus handing on. Her instinct is to pass on habits of checking with your own eyes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. I'd lose the chance to finish my apprenticeship, and the young ones would have no time to plan. What would help is the union having a real say, a guarantee that humans stay on the crews for safety, and a pension bridge so older workers can step aside without losing out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask why a 58-year-old woman climbs poles. People assume it's money, and it isn't. I've got enough. I'm doing it because I can, and I'd like whoever makes these decisions to remember there are people in this trade for reasons a machine wouldn't understand.

headlineQuote: I'm doing it because I can, and I'd like whoever makes these decisions to remember there are people in this trade for reasons a machine wouldn't understand.
portrait: Daria Young is a 58-year-old apprentice lineworker at a publicly owned utility, who carried mail for 31 years before taking her postal pension and following her late brother into the trade. She's slow up a pole, keeps a handwritten notebook and won't touch the crew tablet. Money isn't her worry, so her fears are about losing the chance to finish what she started and about the young apprentices. The two-year AGI picture angers her and pushes her toward the union and early retirement, while five and ten years let her earn her journeyman card and hand the trade on.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she'd lose the chance to finish her apprenticeship and the young workers would have no time to plan.
whatWouldHelp: A real say for the union, a guarantee that humans stay on crews for safety, and a pension bridge so older workers can step aside without losing out.
